"Bearing in mind the rule that the legislation of Congress is to be construed in the interest of the Indian, it may fairly be held that the statute does not contemplate a surrender of jurisdiction"
Alaska Pacific Fisheries v. United States
“the general rule that statutes passed for the benefit of dependent Indian tribes or communities are to be liberally construed, doubtful expressions being resolved in favor of the Indians.”

we must be guided by that "eminently sound and vital canon," ... that "statutes passed for the benefit of dependent Indian tribes . . . are to be liberally construed, doubtful expressions being resolved in favor of the Indians."
“The general rule, entitled to the broadest possible scope, is that in interpreting these Acts legal ambiguities are resolved to the benefit of the Indians.”
"'statutes passed for the benefit of dependent Indian tribes . . . are to be liberally construed, doubtful expressions being resolved in favor of the Indians.'"

“Congressional intent to authorize the extin-guishment of Indian title must be plain and unambiguous… that is, it either must be expressed on the face of the Act or be clear from the surrounding circumstances and legislative history”

“under this Courts traditional approach to statutes regulating Indian affairs”
